title: Pompeii & Vesuvius
keyIdea: Pompeii was a busy Roman town in Italy near a mountain called Vesuvius. In AD 79 Vesuvius erupted. Lava did not reach the town: a giant cloud dropped pumice stones and ash on it for many hours, then clouds of red-hot ash and gas rushed over it and buried it 4 to 6 metres deep. The ash shut out air, rain and people, so it kept buildings, paintings, bread and even the shapes of people and animals, whose bodies left hollows that archaeologists later filled with plaster. The town lay hidden and forgotten for about 1,700 years until digging began in 1748. Because a whole town was frozen in time, its finds show how ordinary Romans lived.
familyTip: Look at photos of Pompeii's streets, the stepping stones and the Beware of the Dog mosaic together. Ask: what does this tell us about the people who lived there?

visual.caption: True about Pompeii or not? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then a box.

items: Ash and pumice buried the town
The ash kept bread and paintings
The town was never found again
The plaster shapes are Roman statues

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap Vesuvius hour by hour, bury things in the ash, make a plaster cast, put the story on a timeline, dig up clues to Roman life.

kid: Long ago, Pompeii was a busy Roman town in Italy. It had shops, bakeries, baths and painted houses. Near the town was a big mountain called Vesuvius. The people did not know it was a volcano.

In AD 79 Vesuvius erupted. A huge cloud of ash and rock shot up into the sky. The wind blew it over Pompeii, and small stones called pumice and ash fell for hours. Many people ran away. The next morning, clouds of red-hot ash rushed down the mountain and covered the town. It was not lava that buried Pompeii. It was ash.

The ash packed tight round everything, like a thick blanket, and went hard. It kept out air and rain. So paintings kept their colours, and loaves of bread kept their shape. Some people and animals could not escape. Their bodies rotted away and left hollows in the ash. Later, people poured plaster into the hollows to see their shapes.

Pompeii stayed hidden under the ground for about 1,700 years. People forgot it was there. In 1748 diggers began to uncover it. Archaeologists are still digging today. The finds are clues that show how Romans lived: what they ate, how they wrote, and even that they kept guard dogs.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This supports the National Curriculum in England for Year 3 rocks and KS2 history (the Roman Empire and its impact), and NGSS 4-ESS3-2 (natural hazards). It is a story topic with a science core: an explosive eruption buries a town in tephra rather than lava. Facts are checked against the Pompeii Archaeological Park, the British Museum, the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and USGS.

The lab has five tasks. Learners tap Vesuvius hour by hour and watch about 3 metres of pumice, then hot ash flows, bury the town. They drop five objects into the ash to see how each was kept. They make a plaster cast in Fiorelli's four steps. They order five story cards from AD 79 to today, and dig up four finds and match each to what it tells us.

Common mistakes. Most children think lava buried Pompeii, as in films. Many think the plaster figures are statues or real people turned to stone. Some think the town was always known, or mix up AD 79 with 1748. Ask: if lava had flowed in, would bread and paintings have survived? Be careful with the date: the eruption is often given as 24 August, but new evidence points to October, so AD 79 is safest.

practice.prompt: What buried the town of Pompeii?
choices: Ash and pumice falling from the sky, then hot ash clouds
Rivers of red-hot lava
A huge wave from the sea
practice.hint: Think about what fell on the houses in the lab.
practice.explain: Pumice and ash fell for hours, then clouds of hot ash rushed over the town. No lava reached Pompeii.

practice.prompt: In a model, ash piles up {n} centimetres every hour for 10 hours. How many centimetres of ash is that?
practice.hint: Multiply the amount each hour by 10 hours.
practice.explain: {n} × 10 = {=n*10} centimetres of ash. It kept piling up, so roofs fell in under the weight.

practice.prompt: Why did paintings and bread last so long at Pompeii?
choices: The ash covered them and kept out air and rain
The Romans painted them with magic paint
People looked after them for 1,700 years
practice.hint: What did the ash do, like a thick blanket?
practice.explain: The ash packed tight round everything and went hard, shutting out air, rain and people, so things kept their shape and colour.

practice.prompt: An archaeologist digs up {a} coins one day and {b} coins the next day. How many coins is that?
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} coins. Coins show which emperors ruled when the town was buried.

practice.prompt: How did archaeologists see the shapes of people buried at Pompeii?
choices: They poured plaster into hollows left in the ash
They found statues the Romans made
The people had turned into stone
practice.hint: What was left when the bodies rotted away?
practice.explain: The bodies rotted and left hollows in the hard ash. Plaster poured in set into their exact shapes.

pool.prompt: In which year did Vesuvius bury Pompeii?
choices: AD 79
pool.hint: Was it in Roman times or when the diggers came?
pool.explain: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, in Roman times. 1748 is when digging began, almost 1,700 years later.

pool.prompt: Put these in order. Which happened first?
choices: Pompeii was a busy Roman town
Diggers started to uncover Pompeii
Archaeologists study Pompeii today
pool.hint: The town had to exist before it could be buried and found.
pool.explain: First the busy Roman town, then the eruption in AD 79, then the digging from 1748, and study today.

pool.prompt: What is the right order to make a plaster cast?
choices: Find a hollow, pour in plaster, let it set, dig away the ash
Dig away the ash, pour in plaster, find a hollow, let it set
Pour in plaster, find a hollow, dig away the ash, let it set
pool.hint: You cannot fill a hollow you have not found yet.
pool.explain: Find the hollow, fill it with plaster, wait for it to set hard, then dig away the ash to see the shape.

pool.prompt: A street in Pompeii has {n} houses on each side. How many houses are on the street?
pool.hint: There are two sides with the same number of houses.
pool.explain: {n} + {n} = {=n*2} houses. Archaeologists give every house a number so they can map the town.

pool.prompt: A baker's oven was found with loaves of bread still inside. What does this tell us?
choices: People bought bread from bakeries
Romans did not eat bread
The volcano baked the bread
pool.hint: Why would one oven be full of loaves?
pool.explain: A bakery made lots of loaves to sell. The 81 loaves found in one oven show bakeries fed the town.

pool.prompt: Why are there big stepping stones across Pompeii's streets?
choices: Streets got wet and dirty, and carts drove between the stones
They were seats for people to rest on
They were left by the volcano
pool.hint: Think about a street after rain with carts going by.
pool.explain: The stones let people cross without stepping in water and dirt, and cart wheels passed in the gaps between them.

pool.prompt: A plaster cast took {d} days to make: 1 day to pour, and the rest to dig. How many days were spent digging?
pool.hint: Take away the 1 day of pouring.
pool.explain: {d} − 1 = {=d-1} days of digging. Digging is slow and careful so the shape does not break.

pool.prompt: Mia says lava buried Pompeii. What is the best answer?
choices: No: ash and pumice fell on it, then hot ash clouds covered it
Yes: lava flowed down and covered every house
No: the sea flooded it
pool.hint: If lava had flowed in, would bread and paintings have survived?
pool.explain: Lava would have burned and melted things. Ash covered the town instead, which is why so much was kept.

pool.prompt: Why can we learn so much about Roman life from Pompeii?
choices: A whole town was buried at once and kept by the ash
It is the only Roman town ever built
The Romans left a guidebook
pool.hint: What makes Pompeii different from towns that slowly fell down?
pool.explain: The ash froze a whole town in time, with homes, shops, food and writing left as they were on one day.
